  "text": "The laundrette clock had been seven minutes fast for as long as Martin could remember.

He liked this. It gave him the small pleasure of leaving earlier than expected.

On Tuesday, a handwritten notice appeared beneath it: CLOSING FRIDAY. THANK YOU FOR 31 YEARS.

Mrs. Shah was folding a towel behind the counter.

“What happens to the machines?” he asked.

“Someone’s collecting them.”

“And the clock?”

She glanced up. “Do you want it?”

He nearly explained that he already had three clocks in his flat, all correct. Instead, he said yes.

Friday evening, he brought his last load. Two shirts, some socks, the blue bedsheet he had washed every week since his divorce.

Mrs. Shah had taken down the price list. A pale rectangle remained on the wall.

While his clothes turned, Martin unscrewed the clock’s bracket with a screwdriver she found in a drawer. Behind the clock was a second pale circle, overlapping an older, smaller one.

“My husband chose that,” she said. “Said people waiting for washing needed numbers they could read.”

Martin lowered it carefully.

At home, he hung it in the kitchen. He reached for the little wheel to correct the time, then left it alone.

The following Tuesday, he carried his washing to the laundrette before remembering.

Mrs. Shah was inside, sweeping.

She unlocked the door when she saw him.

“Habit,” he said, lifting the bag.

“I know. I came in at six.”

He leaned his bag against the counter and asked where she kept the dustpan.

She pointed behind the door, exactly where it had always been."
